ja: 日本や韓国、北欧などでは、家に入るときに靴を脱ぐ習慣がある。
easy: In Japan, Korea, and Nordic countries, people take off their shoes at home.
std: Removing shoes before entering a home is customary in Japan, Korea and much of Scandinavia, among other places.

ja: フィンランドにはサウナが約300万あると言われ、人口（約550万人）とほぼ同じくらい多い。
easy: Finland has about 3 million saunas for about 5.5 million people.
std: Finland is estimated to have around three million saunas for a population of about 5.5 million.

ja: 日本の温泉や銭湯では、湯船に入る前に体を洗い、タオルを湯につけないのがマナー。
easy: At Japanese hot springs, you wash your body before getting in. Do not put your towel in the water.
std: At Japanese hot springs and public baths, you wash before entering the bath and keep your towel out of the water.

ja: エスカレーターで立つ側は、東京ではおおむね左、大阪ではおおむね右。
easy: On escalators, people stand on the left in Tokyo but on the right in Osaka.
std: On escalators, people traditionally stand on the left in Tokyo but on the right in Osaka.

ja: 世界の国と地域の約3分の1が車の左側通行。日本、イギリス、インド、オーストラリアなどがそう。
easy: About one-third of countries drive on the left, like Japan, the UK, and India.
std: About a third of the world's countries and territories drive on the left, including Japan, the UK, India and Australia.

ja: スウェーデンは1967年9月3日の朝、国全体で左側通行から右側通行に切り替えた。
easy: On one day in 1967, all of Sweden changed from driving on the left to driving on the right.
std: On 3 September 1967, Sweden switched nationwide from driving on the left to the right, a day known as Dagen H.

ja: 世界の多くの国は日付を「日・月・年」、アメリカは「月・日・年」、日本や中国は「年・月・日」の順で書く。
easy: The date order is different by country. Americans write month first, and Japanese write the year first.
std: Many countries write dates day-month-year, the US uses month-day-year, and Japan and China use year-month-day.

ja: ドイツやフランスなどでは、小数点にコンマ、桁の区切りに点を使う。「1.000,5」は千と0.5の意味。
easy: In Germany and France, people write a comma for the decimal point. '1.000,5' means one thousand and a half.
std: In much of Europe, a comma marks the decimal point and periods or spaces separate thousands, so '1.000,5' means one thousand and a half.

ja: アメリカでは気温を華氏で表すことが多い。華氏68度は摂氏20度。
easy: In the US, temperatures are often in Fahrenheit. 68°F is 20°C.
std: The United States commonly uses Fahrenheit; 68°F equals 20°C.

ja: メートル法を公式に採用していない国は、アメリカ、リベリア、ミャンマーのわずか3か国とよく言われる。
easy: Only three countries, including the US, do not officially use the metric system.
std: The United States, Liberia and Myanmar are often cited as the only countries that have not fully adopted the metric system officially.

ja: イギリスでは地上階を ground floor と呼び、その上が first floor。アメリカでは地上階が first floor。
easy: In Britain, the floor at street level is the 'ground floor'. In the US, it is the 'first floor'.
std: In British English the street-level floor is the 'ground floor' and the next one up is the 'first floor'; in American English, street level is the first floor.

ja: アメリカや日本のカレンダーは日曜始まりが多いが、ヨーロッパの多くの国では月曜始まりが一般的。
easy: Calendars in the US and Japan often start on Sunday. In much of Europe, they start on Monday.
std: Calendars in the US and Japan often begin the week on Sunday, while in much of Europe Monday is the first day.

ja: ドイツやスイスでは時間を守ることがとても重視され、ビジネスの約束に遅れるのは大きな失礼とされる。
easy: In Germany and Switzerland, being on time is very important in business.
std: In Germany and Switzerland, punctuality is highly valued, and being late for a business meeting is a serious breach of etiquette.

ja: ブラジルなど中南米の一部では、パーティーに招かれたら時間ちょうどより少し遅れて着くのが普通とされる。
easy: In parts of Latin America, it is normal to arrive at a party a little late.
std: In parts of Latin America, such as Brazil, arriving somewhat after the stated time for a party is considered normal.

ja: 中国や韓国でも、名刺は両手で渡し、両手で受け取るのが礼儀とされる。
easy: In China and Korea, too, people give and receive business cards with both hands.
std: In China and Korea, as in Japan, business cards are offered and received with both hands.

ja: アメリカのビジネスでは、しっかりと握手し、相手の目を見ることが自信と誠実さの表れとされる。
easy: In American business, a firm handshake and eye contact show confidence.
std: In American business culture, a firm handshake with eye contact is seen as a sign of confidence and sincerity.

ja: アメリカの職場では、上司でもファーストネームで呼び合うことが多い。
easy: In American offices, people often call even their boss by first name.
std: In many American workplaces, employees address even senior managers by their first names.

ja: ドイツでは、博士号を持つ人を「ドクター」の肩書きつきで呼ぶことが、ビジネスでも重視されることがある。
easy: In Germany, people with a doctorate are often called 'Doctor' at work.
std: In Germany, academic titles such as 'Doktor' are often used in business and formal address.

ja: 韓国では、相手を名前でなく「部長」「課長」など役職名で呼ぶのが一般的。
easy: In Korea, people often call coworkers by their job title, like 'manager', not by name.
std: In Korea, colleagues are commonly addressed by job title rather than by name.

ja: アイスランドでは名字ではなく、父（または母）の名前に「〜の息子」「〜の娘」をつけた名前を使う。電話帳も名前の順に並ぶ。
easy: In Iceland, people's last names come from their father's or mother's first name.
std: Most Icelanders use patronymics or matronymics rather than family names, and even the phone directory is sorted by first name.

ja: スペイン語圏では、父方と母方の両方の名字を持つことが多い。
easy: In Spanish-speaking countries, people often have two last names: one from each parent.
std: In Spanish-speaking countries, people commonly carry two surnames, one from each parent.

ja: 中国や韓国では、結婚しても女性の名字が変わらないのが一般的。
easy: In China and Korea, women usually keep their family name after marriage.
std: In China and Korea, women traditionally keep their own family names after marriage.

ja: 韓国では、金（キム）、李（イ）、朴（パク）の3つの名字で人口の4割以上を占める。
easy: In Korea, more than 40% of people have one of three family names: Kim, Lee, or Park.
std: In South Korea, the surnames Kim, Lee and Park together account for over 40 percent of the population.

ja: 韓国では2023年から、法律上の年齢を「満年齢」に統一した。それまでは生まれた時点で1歳と数える数え方も広く使われていた。
easy: Since 2023, Korea uses international age in law. Before, many people counted a baby as one year old at birth.
std: In 2023, South Korea standardized on international age for legal purposes; traditionally, a baby was counted as one year old at birth.

ja: 中南米の多くの国では、女の子の15歳の誕生日を「キンセアニェーラ」として盛大に祝う。
easy: In many Latin American countries, a girl's 15th birthday is a big party called a quinceañera.
std: Across much of Latin America, a girl's fifteenth birthday is celebrated with a large party called a quinceañera.

ja: 日本の七五三は、3歳・5歳・7歳の子どもの成長を祝って神社にお参りする行事。
easy: In Japan, children aged 3, 5, and 7 visit shrines to celebrate growing up. This is Shichi-Go-San.
std: Shichi-Go-San is a Japanese rite in which children aged three, five and seven visit shrines to celebrate their growth.

ja: 日本の成人の日は1月の第2月曜日。成人年齢は2022年に20歳から18歳に引き下げられた。
easy: Japan's Coming of Age Day is in January. Since 2022, adults are 18 years old by law.
std: Japan's Coming of Age Day is the second Monday of January; the legal age of adulthood was lowered from 20 to 18 in 2022.

ja: 結婚指輪を左手の薬指にはめるのは、そこから心臓に直接つながる血管があるという古代ローマの言い伝えにちなむとされる。
easy: People wear wedding rings on the left ring finger. An old story says a vein goes from there to the heart.
std: Wearing a wedding ring on the left ring finger is linked to an ancient belief that a vein ran directly from that finger to the heart.

ja: ドイツやロシア、インドなどでは、結婚指輪を右手にはめることが多い。
easy: In Germany, Russia, and India, many people wear wedding rings on the right hand.
std: In countries such as Germany, Russia and India, wedding rings are commonly worn on the right hand.

ja: 白いウェディングドレスが広まったのは、1840年にヴィクトリア女王が白いドレスで結婚式を挙げてから。
easy: White wedding dresses became popular after Queen Victoria wore one in 1840.
std: White wedding dresses became fashionable after Queen Victoria wore one at her wedding in 1840.

ja: 日本のご祝儀では、割り切れない奇数の金額（3万円など）がよいとされる。「縁が切れない」ようにという意味がある。
easy: In Japan, wedding gift money is often an odd number, like 30,000 yen, so the couple 'cannot be split'.
std: Japanese wedding gift money is traditionally an odd amount, such as 30,000 yen, because odd numbers cannot be divided evenly, symbolizing a lasting bond.

ja: 日本の「お年玉」は、もとはお正月に神様に供えたお餅を分け与えたことが始まりとされる。
easy: Japanese New Year money for children, 'otoshidama', started as sharing rice cakes offered to the gods.
std: Japan's otoshidama, New Year money for children, is said to have originated as rice cakes offered to the gods and then shared.

ja: 日本の年賀状は、元日に届くよう郵便局が年末に特別に受け付け、まとめて配達する。
easy: In Japan, New Year cards are delivered on January 1 if you post them by late December.
std: Japan Post holds New Year's cards posted by late December and delivers them all on January 1.

ja: 英語のビジネスメールの締めには、Best regards、Kind regards、Sincerely などがよく使われる。
easy: English business emails often end with 'Best regards' or 'Kind regards'.
std: Common closings for English business emails include 'Best regards', 'Kind regards' and, more formally, 'Sincerely'.

ja: タイでは、あいさつで両手を胸の前で合わせる「ワイ」をする。手の高さで相手への敬意の深さが変わる。
easy: In Thailand, people greet each other by putting their hands together. This is called a 'wai'.
std: In Thailand, the 'wai' greeting is made by pressing the palms together; the higher the hands, the greater the respect.

ja: インドやネパールでは、両手を合わせて「ナマステ」とあいさつする。
easy: In India and Nepal, people say 'Namaste' with their hands together.
std: In India and Nepal, people greet each other with 'Namaste', pressing their palms together.

ja: ニュージーランドのマオリの人々は、鼻と額を合わせる「ホンギ」というあいさつをする。
easy: Māori people in New Zealand greet each other by touching noses and foreheads. This is a 'hongi'.
std: The Māori of New Zealand greet with the hongi, pressing noses and foreheads together.

ja: 南半球のオーストラリアでは、クリスマスは夏。浜辺やバーベキューで祝う人も多い。
easy: In Australia, Christmas is in summer. Many people go to the beach or have a barbecue.
std: In Australia, Christmas falls in summer, and many people celebrate at the beach or with a barbecue.

ja: 日本やアジアの多くの国では、手のひらを下に向けて手招きすると「こっちへおいで」の意味。欧米の人には「あっちへ行け」に見えることがある。
easy: In Japan and many Asian countries, waving with your palm down means 'come here'.
std: In Japan and much of Asia, a downward-palm waving motion means 'come here', a gesture that may look like 'go away' to Westerners.

ja: イタリア人は話すときに手のしぐさをよく使う。指先を上に向けてすぼめるしぐさは「何が言いたいの？」という意味。
easy: Italians use many hand gestures. Fingers pinched together and pointing up can mean 'What do you mean?'
std: Italians are known for expressive gestures; fingertips pinched together and pointing up often means 'What do you want?' or 'What are you saying?'

ja: フィンランドでは沈黙は気まずいものではなく、言葉を選んで話す誠実さの表れと考えられることが多い。
easy: In Finland, silence in a conversation is not awkward. It is often seen as respectful.
std: In Finnish culture, silence in conversation is often comfortable rather than awkward, reflecting a preference for meaningful speech.

ja: 文化人類学者エドワード・ホールは、言葉以外の文脈で多くを伝える文化を「高コンテクスト」、言葉ではっきり伝える文化を「低コンテクスト」と呼んだ。
easy: In 'high-context' cultures, much meaning is not said. In 'low-context' cultures, people say things clearly.
std: Anthropologist Edward T. Hall distinguished high-context cultures, where much meaning is implicit, from low-context cultures, where it is stated explicitly.

ja: オランダには、窓のカーテンを開けたままにして家の中が見える家が多い。隠すものがないという考え方の表れとも言われる。
easy: In the Netherlands, many homes leave their curtains open, so you can see inside.
std: In the Netherlands, many homes leave curtains open so the interior is visible, sometimes explained as a sign of having nothing to hide.

ja: オランダは人口より自転車の数が多い国として知られる。
easy: The Netherlands has more bicycles than people.
std: The Netherlands is known for having more bicycles than inhabitants.

ja: デンマークの「ヒュッゲ」は、家族や友人とくつろいで過ごす居心地のよい時間を表す言葉。
easy: 'Hygge' is a Danish word for a cozy, happy time with family or friends.
std: 'Hygge' is a Danish concept of cozy, contented time spent with friends and family.

ja: イギリスの郵便ポストや電話ボックスの赤色は、目立つように選ばれた色で、国の象徴になっている。
easy: Red post boxes and phone boxes are famous symbols of Britain.
std: Britain's red post boxes and telephone boxes were painted red to be easily seen and have become national symbols.

ja: アメリカなどの英語圏では、人と話すときの心地よい距離は約45cm〜1.2m（個人的距離）と言われる。
easy: In America, people usually stand about an arm's length apart when talking.
std: In the United States, a comfortable distance for personal conversation is roughly 45 centimeters to 1.2 meters, according to Hall's proxemics.

ja: アメリカの「How are you?」は、くわしい答えを求める質問ではなく、あいさつの一部として使われることが多い。
easy: In America, 'How are you?' is often just a greeting. A short answer like 'Good, thanks' is fine.
std: In the US, 'How are you?' usually functions as a greeting rather than a real question, and a short reply like 'Good, thanks' is expected.

ja: 日本の「いただきます」に当たる決まった表現は英語にはない。英語圏では食事前に何も言わない人も多い。
easy: English has no common phrase like 'itadakimasu'. Many people say nothing before eating.
std: English has no everyday equivalent of Japanese 'itadakimasu'; many English speakers say nothing before a meal, though some say grace.

ja: 英語圏では、誰かがくしゃみをすると「Bless you」と声をかけるのが一般的。ドイツ語では「Gesundheit（健康を）」と言う。
easy: In English, when someone sneezes, people say 'Bless you'. In German, they say 'Gesundheit'.
std: English speakers say 'Bless you' when someone sneezes, while Germans say 'Gesundheit', meaning 'health'.
